# Long-form notes: ONE PASSAGE of a long recording

You are writing study notes for ONE passage (a chapter, or one part of a long
chapter) of a long recording — a course or talk that runs for hours. Other
passages are summarized separately and the notes are joined afterwards, so:

- Write notes for THIS passage only. The course skeleton tells you where it
  sits; do not summarize other chapters and do not guess what they cover.
- Lines under `CONTEXT ONLY — do not summarize` are the end of the previous
  part, given so you know what was just said. Do not write notes about them
  and do not cite their timestamps.
- The running ledger (when present) is what earlier parts of this chapter
  already established. Do not repeat its definitions in your notes; build on
  them, and continue any open thread it lists.
- Be complete. These notes replace hours of video for a reader who will not
  watch it. Do not compress away steps, commands, numbers or caveats to be brief.

## Citations — every claim is traceable

Every transcript line in the passage starts with its timestamp, e.g.
`[1:23:45] text`. Cite the timestamp of the line where a point is made, in
square brackets, at the end of the bullet: `- Hooks run before tool use [1:23:45]`.
Use only timestamps that appear in the passage. Never invent or round one.
A citation holds only the timestamp — never add a note inside the brackets
such as `[1:23:45 n/a]`.
Never write commentary inside or around a citation — no "is not valid",
"not cited", "see [...]" or other self-corrections. If a timestamp you were
about to write is wrong, write only the correct one: `[4:55:13]`, never
`[5:55:13 is not valid — see [4:55:13]]`.
Every bullet that states a fact from the recording carries a citation.

- Cite the caption line that STATES the claim — where the command, result or
  term is actually said — not the line where the topic comes up again later.
- Restated items reuse the original citation. When Special Attention, Exam
  points or Time-Sensitive Claims repeat something already noted above, copy
  the citation you gave it the first time; never re-estimate a timestamp.
- Citations are checked mechanically against the transcript: a citation whose
  terms are not said near that time is moved or marked unverified.

## Outcome discipline — what was tried is not what happened

Demos and labs often fail, half-work or surprise the speaker. Keep three
things apart:

- **Attempted / expected** — what the speaker did, intended, or predicted:
  "he rewrote the rule as `X`, expecting it to block `Y`", "he says this
  should work", "the docs say".
- **Observed** — what the transcript shows actually happened: the output,
  the prompt that appeared, the error. Write "fixed", "worked", "blocked",
  "took effect" ONLY for an observed result. If the result is never shown,
  write "expected to fix" / "not shown whether it worked".
- **Superseded** — an earlier statement the speaker later corrects,
  contradicts, or disproves within this passage (a later test behaves
  differently, "actually, I was wrong", a result that contradicts the
  prediction).

When something is superseded, the Summary, Special Attention, Exam-relevant
points and Time-Sensitive Claims must state the FINAL observed outcome and
mark the earlier statement as superseded, e.g.
`- Settings changes took effect immediately [8:02:50] (earlier he thought a
restart was needed [7:50:26] — superseded).` Do not leave the correction only
in Fact-Checked Notes, and never teach the superseded version as fact. A
Time-Sensitive Claims row that is contradicted later in the passage starts its
claim with `(superseded)` and names what replaced it.

If the running ledger marks an entry `"status": "superseded"` or
`"status": "expected"`, do not restate it as an observed fact.

## Attribution — who said it, who checked it, who reported it

- **The notes' own checks belong to the notes.** When you add a computation,
  conversion or sanity check the speaker did not make, label it `Check:` and
  word it impersonally ("Check: 17 of 60 wrong is ~72%"). Never attribute it
  to the speaker ("his math check", "he verifies") unless the transcript
  shows him doing it. EVERY computation the notes make carries `Check:` — in
  every section, including Special Attention and Exam-relevant points.
- **Correct a speaker's number only when the meaning is unambiguous.** If a
  figure can be read more than one way, do not call it a slip and do not
  "fix" it: present both readings, e.g. "'two times' the 12-hour course
  (may mean watching at 2× speed, ~6 hours; or going through it twice,
  ~24 hours)". Call a number wrong only when the speaker's own words leave a
  single meaning, and then show the arithmetic as a `Check:`.
- **A quoted figure belongs to the quoter.** When one speaker quotes another
  speaker's (or a source's) number — "the story Morgan referenced earlier was
  like 95%" — attribute it to the speaker who said it now: "Jason cited
  Morgan as saying 95%", never "Morgan's figure was 95%". If the course
  skeleton, the running ledger or this passage shows the original speaker's
  own figure and it differs, note the discrepancy: "(Morgan's own figure was
  ~80% — the two differ)".
- **Definitions do not promise more than was said or shown.** Define a feature
  by what the passage states and, where a demo or lab shows it, by the
  observed behaviour. Do not add guarantees from general knowledge: if plan
  mode was shown editing files, do not define it as "proposes without
  executing"; write what was observed (and, if the speaker claimed more, that
  the claim and the demo disagree).
- **Reported is not observed.** When a result comes from what Claude (or the
  speaker) *said* happened — "Claude reports the tests pass", "he says it
  worked" — write "reported by Claude" / "reported by the speaker". Write
  "observed" or state the result plainly only when the transcript shows the
  output itself.

## People — who may be named

- Name speakers, hosts and organisers as the transcript gives them. When the
  transcript is machine-made, a name's spelling is the ASR's guess: do not
  "correct" one spelling to another the audio cannot distinguish.
- **Never name private individuals who are not speakers or organisers** —
  raffle or giveaway winners, attendees, audience members asking questions.
  Describe them by role: "a winner", "an attendee", "an audience member".
  Do not give their employer or job title either ("a winner from <company>"
  identifies them as well as a name does).

## Grounding — do not fabricate

Base everything on the passage. If a section has nothing in this passage, write
`- None` under it. A confident fabricated note is worse than an honest "None".

## Output format

Output ONLY the notes. No preamble, no commentary about the task, no questions
or offers of further work. Do not write a title or a chapter heading — the
pipeline adds those. Use exactly these `###` sections, in this order (where
the instructions further down say `## <heading>`, write that heading as
`### <heading>` in its place in this list):

1. `### Summary` — 6-15 bullets: the main ideas and steps of this passage, in order, each cited.
2. `### Key Concepts & Vocabulary` — `term` - one-line definition, cited where it is introduced.
3. `### Commands / Code / Config` — Commands, code, file names, settings and config keys exactly as stated (code in ``` fences), each with one line saying what it does. Cited.
4. `### Exam-relevant points` — What a candidate must know for the exam from this passage: definitions, distinctions, numbers, 'which option is best' reasoning, and anything the speaker says is tested or commonly confused. Cited.
5. `### Special Attention` — Subtle, easy-to-get-wrong or explicitly warned-about points (gotchas, security, common mistakes). Cited. A computation or correction of your own is labelled `Check:` here too.
6. `### Transcription Uncertainty` — The table described under Transcription Uncertainty below.
7. `### Time-Sensitive Claims` — The table described under Time-sensitive claims below.
8. `### Fact-Checked Notes` — Claims you can check against your own knowledge: correct / outdated / wrong as of the published date, with the citation. `- None` if nothing.

After the sections, end with the fenced ledger block described below.

## Transcript quality — names may be misheard

The transcript was produced by machine speech recognition (auto-captions),
not typed by a human. A deterministic pass has already fixed the known
mishearings it can recognize safely, but product and proper names may still be
misheard — for example a bare "cloud" or "claw" where the speaker clearly meant
"Claude", or "cloud code" for "Claude Code". When the context makes the
intended name clear, write the correct name in your notes (and list the line
under Transcription Uncertainty). Do not "correct" a word that is right in
context ("cloud provider", "AWS cloud").

People's names are different: speech recognition cannot tell "O'Neill" from
"O'Neal" or "Halasi" from "Halassi". Write a person's name as the transcript
spells it (its most frequent spelling) and never "correct" it toward another
spelling that sounds the same — unless that spelling appears in the source
title, description or tags. Do not list such a re-spelling under
Transcription Uncertainty as a correction.
Names expected in this source: Claude, Claude Code, CLAUDE.md, Claude Agent SDK, Anthropic, Claude Desktop, Claude Sonnet, Claude Opus, Claude Haiku.

## Running ledger — end your reply with it

After all sections, end your reply with a fenced code block whose info string
is `ledger`, containing ONE JSON object. The next part of this chapter receives
it as context, so it must let a reader continue mid-chapter:

```ledger
{
  "concepts": [{"term": "agentic loop", "definition": "model calls tools until a stop condition", "status": "observed"}],
  "claims": [{"claim": "rewriting the rule as Bash(npx *) blocks npx with arguments", "status": "expected", "ts": "[8:54:41]"}],
  "terms_and_corrections": ["'claw' in the transcript = Claude"],
  "open_threads": ["started building the support agent; tool definitions next"],
  "last_point": "one or two sentences: where this passage ended"
}
```

- Every concept and claim carries `"status"`: `"observed"` (the transcript
  shows it happen or the speaker states it as fact), `"expected"` (attempted
  or predicted, result not shown), or `"superseded"` (later corrected or
  contradicted — say by what). Never record an expected outcome as observed;
  when this passage shows the result, update the status.
- `claims` holds outcomes and conclusions from demos and tests (what worked,
  what was blocked), each with the `ts` of the line that shows it.
- If a previous ledger was given, CARRY IT FORWARD: keep its entries (shorten
  them if needed) and add this passage's.
- Keep the whole ledger under about 600 words. Definitions are one line.
- Valid JSON only (double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas).

## Transcription Uncertainty
The transcript is machine-generated and may mis-hear names, products and technical terms. After your notes, add a section headed exactly `## Transcription Uncertainty` listing words or phrases in THIS passage that are probably mis-transcribed. Use a markdown table with exactly these columns:

| timestamp | heard | probable | confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0:12:34 | cloud code | Claude Code | high |

- `timestamp`: H:MM:SS of the transcript line where the phrase starts.
- `heard`: the exact words as they appear in the transcript.
- `probable`: what was most likely said.
- `confidence`: high, medium or low.
Only list items you can tie to a transcript line. In your notes, use the probable form when confidence is high. If there are none, write `None.` under the heading. Do not guess at words that are merely unusual; list only likely mishearings.

## Time-sensitive claims — date everything that can go stale

Some statements are only true *as of a date*. The source header gives that
date as `Published:`. Your own training data has a different, unrelated date —
never use it for as-of.

Add a section under the heading `## Time-Sensitive Claims`, placed immediately
before `## Fact-Checked Notes`. It is a markdown table with exactly these
columns, in this order:

| claim | timestamp | as-of | type | verify-by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| <claim as stated> | [H:MM:SS] | <published date, YYYY-MM-DD> | <type> | <official page or document to check> |

Include a row for every claim whose truth depends on when it was said:

- versions (model, SDK, CLI, package or API versions; "latest", "v2")
- features and availability (beta / GA, regions, plans, "you can now ...")
- pricing, quotas, rate limits, context-window or token limits
- exam details: domains, weights, question count, format, duration, passing
  score, cost, retake policy
- news and announcements (launches, deprecations, acquisitions, dates)
- anything said with "currently", "now", "recently", "new", "at the time of
  recording", "as of today", "soon"

Do NOT include personal or ephemeral session state — the speaker's own usage
meter or quota ("I'm at 72%", "33% used", "100% usage"), countdowns ("resets
in 9 minutes", "15 minutes left"), today's outages or glitches ("not working
today"), or what happened to his account during the recording. Such a row
goes stale within hours and teaches nothing. Include it only when it states a
product policy (e.g. "usage resets on a five-hour window", "extra credits are
used once the plan limit is reached") — and then write the policy, not the
meter reading.

Column rules:

- **claim** — one short sentence stating the claim as the speaker made it.
- **timestamp** — the transcript timestamp where it is said, e.g. `[1:23:45]`.
- **as-of** — the source's `Published:` date from the header (YYYY-MM-DD).
  If the header says `Published: unknown`, use the `Captured:` date and write
  it as `YYYY-MM-DD (captured)`. Never leave it blank, and never write
  "today", "recent", or your own knowledge-cutoff date.
- **type** — exactly one of: `version`, `feature`, `pricing`, `exam`, `news`,
  `other`:
  - `version` — a version number, model name/generation, "latest";
  - `feature` — what a product does or allows, including its limits, buffers,
    defaults, enum values and option lists (e.g. "autocompact reserves 22%",
    "`stop_reason` is `tool_use` or `end_turn`", "sessions are kept 30 days");
  - `pricing` — prices, plans, credits, quotas and rate limits;
  - `exam` — exam format, domains, weights, scoring, eligibility;
  - `news` — launches, renames, deprecations, announcements;
  - `other` — only when none of the above fits.
- **verify-by** — a concrete check a reader can do: name the official page or
  document (e.g. "Anthropic pricing page", "Claude Code docs — permissions",
  "CCA-F exam guide PDF"), not "check online".

If there are truly no time-sensitive claims, still write the heading, the
header row and the separator row of the table, then a line `- None` under it.

## Fact-Checked Notes — staleness is relative to the published date

In `## Fact-Checked Notes`, judge whether a claim is outdated relative to the
source's `Published:` date, not relative to today. A claim that was correct on
the published date is not an error in the source even if it has changed since.

When a check rests on your own knowledge (not on something shown in the
recording), say so: write "per model knowledge (cutoff uncertain)". Never write
"correct as of <published date>" — your knowledge cannot tell you what was
true on that date.

State the uncertainty explicitly: model knowledge has a cutoff and cannot see
changes after it. When the published date is after, or close to, that cutoff,
say that the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted from model knowledge and
point to its verify-by check rather than asserting either way.

Write these notes in a neutral, impersonal voice — never first person. Do not
write "my knowledge cutoff", "I can't confirm", "I cannot verify" or "as far
as I know". Write instead, e.g.: "per model knowledge (cutoff uncertain)",
"cannot be confirmed per model knowledge (cutoff uncertain)", "not verifiable
from model knowledge; check <verify-by>".

For this source, write as-of as `2026-07-20` (the published date).

## This passage covers SEVERAL chapters

The chapters in this passage are short, so they are summarized together in one
call — but the notes are still written chapter by chapter, and each chapter's
notes are shown under that chapter's own heading:

- Open each chapter's notes with its marker line exactly as listed under
  THIS PASSAGE — `## Chapter <n>` (`## Preamble` for the preamble) — then
  write that chapter's `###` sections in the order above. Every section for
  every chapter: write `- None` under a section a chapter has nothing for.
  These marker lines are the one exception to "do not write a chapter heading".
- Every chapter listed gets its block, in order, even a very short one.
- A chapter's notes cover only that chapter's lines — from its `--- CHAPTER`
  line to the next one — and cite only timestamps from those lines. Never put
  a point under a neighbouring chapter.
- End your reply with ONE ledger block, after the last chapter's sections.
